name: Repair a control-plane component
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Maintenance & Troubleshooting. Drill EVERY node-level cluster-ops corner harder than the exam: static pods and mirror pods, repairing a crash-looping control-plane component, etcd snapshot backup, node taints and labels, cordon/drain for maintenance, uncordon to return a node, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly on persistent node/cluster state via docker exec and kubectl -o json.

questions.title: Repair a crash-looping control-plane component
questions.teach:
The control-plane (apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd) also runs as **static pods** from `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on `$CP`. A bad flag crash-loops one; fix the manifest **on the node** and the kubelet restarts it in ~15s.

**Gotcha:** diagnose with `kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$CP` (shows the bad flag); kind nodes have **no vi/nano**, so edit with `sed`, and never `kubectl edit` (mirror pods are read-only).

**When kubectl itself is dead:** if the broken component is the **apiserver or etcd**, `kubectl` stops answering — so you can't read logs that way. Shell onto `$CP` and diagnose from the container runtime instead: `crictl ps -a` (find the crash-looping container), `crictl logs <id>`, and `journalctl -u kubelet`. See the 🧰 **Node toolbox** above for the full set.
questions.prompt:
Setup injected a bogus flag into the **kube-scheduler** static pod manifest on `$CP`, so the scheduler crash-loops. Fix `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` on `$CP` so the scheduler becomes healthy.

Target: the `kube-scheduler-$CP` pod in `kube-system` is Ready (1/1) and the bogus flag is gone.
questions.hint: Diagnose: `kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$CP` → `unknown flag: --bogus-flag`. Then shell onto the node (exam: `ssh <node>`; here `docker exec -it $CP bash`), `cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/`, and remove that line with `sed` (no vi on kind nodes). Kubelet restarts it in ~15s.
questions.solution:
# 1) diagnose — the logs name the bad flag
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$CP | tail      # Error: unknown flag: --bogus-flag

# 2) shell onto the control-plane node (exam equivalent: ssh <node>)
docker exec -it $CP bash
cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# kind nodes have no vi/nano — edit with sed (or: apt-get update && apt-get install -y vim)
sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' kube-scheduler.yaml
exit

# 3) back on base: watch it recover
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-scheduler-$CP -w

verification.description: kube-scheduler static pod Ready again, bogus flag removed

questions.eli5:
Think of your cluster's "brain" — the API server, scheduler, controller-manager, and etcd — as four essential staff members running a restaurant. On a kind cluster they aren't hired through the normal scheduler at all. Instead, the kitchen manager (the **kubelet** on the control-plane node) reads their job descriptions from a special folder on the node, `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/`, and starts each one automatically. These are called **static pods**.

Imagine someone sneaked into that folder and scribbled a nonsense instruction into the scheduler's job description ("do a backflip" / `--bogus-flag`). Every time the scheduler tries to start, it reads the gibberish, throws up its hands, and quits — over and over. That's a **crash loop**.

To fix it you read the complaint first: `kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$CP` prints `unknown flag: --bogus-flag`. Then you go to the folder itself and erase that bad line from the file. The moment you save, the kitchen manager notices the job description changed and restarts the worker — healthy again in about 15 seconds.

**Watch out:**

- You **cannot** `kubectl edit` a static pod. What the API shows is a **mirror pod** — a read-only photocopy. The real file lives on the node; edit it there.
- **kind nodes have no `vi` or `nano`.** Edit with `sed`, or install an editor.
- If the broken component is the **apiserver or etcd**, `kubectl` itself goes silent (the brain is down). Shell onto the node and use `crictl ps -a`, `crictl logs <id>`, and `journalctl -u kubelet` instead.
- Don't move or rename the manifest file — just fix the bad line. A missing file makes the kubelet **delete** the component entirely.
questions.deepDive:
## Repairing a crash-looping control-plane component — full rundown

### Mental model
A kubeadm control plane runs its core components — **kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, and etcd** — as **static pods**. The kubelet on the control-plane node watches `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` and runs whatever Pod manifests it finds there. The API server exposes a read-only **mirror pod** named `<pod>-<nodeName>` so you can *see* the pod, but the source of truth is the file on disk. Fix the file → the kubelet reconciles within ~15–20s.

### Where things live (control-plane node)
| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` | apiserver static pod |
| `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` | scheduler static pod |
| `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml` | controller-manager static pod |
| `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml` | etcd static pod |
| `/etc/kubernetes/pki/` | cluster certs/keys |
| `/var/log/pods/`, `/var/log/containers/` | component logs on the node |

### Diagnose
```bash
# which component is unhealthy?
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide

# read the failing component's logs (works while apiserver is up)
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$CP | tail
# -> Error: unknown flag: --bogus-flag
```

When `kubectl` is **dead** (apiserver or etcd broken), diagnose from the node's runtime:
```bash
# exam: ssh <node>   |   kind: docker exec -it $CP bash
crictl ps -a | grep kube-scheduler          # find the exited/crash-looping container
crictl logs <container-id> | tail            # same error, straight from containerd
journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail   # kubelet's view of why it won't stay up
```

### Fix (edit the manifest on the node)
```bash
docker exec -it $CP bash                     # exam: ssh <node>
cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

# kind nodes have NO vi/nano — use sed, or install one:
#   apt-get update && apt-get install -y vim
grep -n bogus kube-scheduler.yaml
sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' kube-scheduler.yaml
exit

# watch the kubelet rebuild it (~15s)
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-scheduler-$CP -w
```

### How the kubelet reacts to manifest changes
| Change to the manifest file | Kubelet action |
|---|---|
| Edit a field | Deletes old container(s), starts new ones (~15s) |
| Remove the file | **Deletes** the static pod + mirror pod |
| Move file back in | Recreates the static pod |
| Syntax error (bad YAML) | Pod not (re)created; error in `journalctl -u kubelet` |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Never `kubectl edit`/`kubectl apply` a static pod.** The API object is a **mirror pod** — read-only. Edits are rejected or silently ineffective. Always edit the file on the node.
- The mirror pod name is `<metadata.name>-<nodeName>`, e.g. `kube-scheduler-cp1`.
- **No editor on kind nodes.** Prefer `sed`. Keep YAML indentation intact — a stray space breaks the manifest.
- If the broken component is **apiserver or etcd**, `kubectl` returns connection errors. Switch to `crictl` + `journalctl` on the node.
- After fixing, the container restart **count** keeps its history — check `READY 1/1` and that the age of the running container is fresh, not the restart count.
- Static-pod directory path is set by the kubelet flag `--pod-manifest-path` or `staticPodPath` in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`; default for kubeadm is `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get pods                       # spot the crash-looper
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$CP | tail  # name the cause
docker exec -it $CP bash                               # ssh <node> in the exam
sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-scheduler-$CP -w   # wait for 1/1 Ready
# apiserver/etcd down? -> crictl ps -a ; crictl logs <id> ; journalctl -u kubelet
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a crash-looping controller-manager (no hint)
questions.teach:
When a control-plane component is unhealthy, `kubectl -n kube-system get pods` shows the crash-looping one; its logs or its manifest on `$CP` reveal the cause. Fix the manifest on the node and let the kubelet restart it.

**Gotcha:** the fault is a bad flag in the manifest — no hint here; find it yourself, then confirm the pod reaches `1/1 Ready`. If a fault ever takes down the apiserver so `kubectl` goes silent, fall back to the node: `crictl ps -a` → `crictl logs <id>` and `journalctl -u kubelet` (🧰 Node toolbox).
questions.prompt:
Setup has broken the **kube-controller-manager** static pod on `$CP`; it is crash-looping. Diagnose the cause and fix it so the component is healthy again. Edit the manifest on the node — do not try `kubectl edit`.

Target: `kube-controller-manager-$CP` in `kube-system` is Ready (1/1).
questions.hint: No hint on the fault — diagnose it: `kubectl -n kube-system get pods` shows the crash; `kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-$CP` (or `crictl logs` on the node) names the cause. Fix the manifest on `$CP` with `sed` (kind has no vi): shell in, `cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/`, remove the bad line.
questions.solution:
# diagnose: logs name the bad flag
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-$CP | tail    # unknown flag: --bogus-flag

# (fallback when kubectl is unavailable — diagnose from the node's runtime)
docker exec $CP crictl ps -a | grep kube-controller-manager        # find the crash-looping container
# docker exec $CP crictl logs <container-id> | tail                # same error, straight from containerd

# fix on the node (no vi on kind -> sed)
docker exec -it $CP bash
cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
grep -n bogus kube-controller-manager.yaml
sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' kube-controller-manager.yaml
exit

kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-controller-manager-$CP -w

verification.description: kube-controller-manager static pod Ready again, fault removed

questions.eli5:
This is the same kind of rescue as before, but now **nobody tells you what broke** — you have to play detective.

Picture the control-plane as a team of specialists. One of them, the **controller-manager** (the member who keeps everything tidy — replacing dead pods, managing node health, driving deployments toward their desired state), has been given a garbled instruction and now keeps quitting the instant it starts. Your job: figure out *why* on your own, then fix it.

Good detectives work in order:

1. **Find the sick one.** `kubectl -n kube-system get pods` — look for the pod that's `0/1`, `CrashLoopBackOff`, or racking up restarts.
2. **Ask it what hurts.** `kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-$CP` — the last lines usually name the exact problem, like `unknown flag: --bogus-flag`.
3. **Fix the source.** The complaint comes from a line in the manifest file on the node. Shell in, open `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml`, remove the bad line, and the kubelet restarts the component in about 15 seconds.

**Watch out:**

- **No hint this time** — read the logs; they almost always name the fault directly.
- It's a **static pod**, so again: edit the file **on the node**, never `kubectl edit`.
- **No `vi` on kind nodes** — use `sed`. Use `grep -n bogus <file>` first to find the exact line.
- If this component being down somehow takes the **apiserver** with it and `kubectl` goes quiet, drop to the node: `crictl ps -a` → `crictl logs <id>`, plus `journalctl -u kubelet`.
- Confirm success by actually seeing `1/1 Ready`, not just "the error stopped scrolling."
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnose & fix a crash-looping control-plane component (no hint) — full rundown

### Mental model
Same machinery as any control-plane repair: the component is a **static pod** run by the kubelet from `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on the control-plane node, surfaced to the API as a read-only **mirror pod** `<pod>-<nodeName>`. The difference here is purely diagnostic — **you are not told what the fault is**, so you follow a repeatable triage path and let the logs tell you.

### What kube-controller-manager does
It runs the built-in controllers that drive actual state toward desired state: node lifecycle, replica/Deployment/ReplicaSet reconciliation, endpoints, service accounts & tokens, PV/PVC binding, and more. When it's down, the cluster keeps serving reads/writes (apiserver is fine) but **stops healing** — crashed pods aren't replaced, scaling stalls, nodes aren't marked NotReady on time.

### The triage ladder (memorize this order)
```bash
# 1. Which component is unhealthy?
kubectl -n kube-system get pods
#   look for 0/1, CrashLoopBackOff, or a climbing RESTARTS count

# 2. Why? Read its logs.
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-$CP | tail
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-$CP --previous | tail   # last crashed instance

# 3. If kubectl is unavailable, go to the node's runtime:
docker exec $CP crictl ps -a | grep kube-controller-manager   # find crash-looping container
docker exec $CP crictl logs <container-id> | tail
docker exec $CP journalctl -u kubelet -e --no-pager | tail
```

### Common fault classes and where they show up
| Symptom in logs | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `unknown flag: --xxx` | bogus/unsupported flag in manifest | delete that flag line |
| `invalid argument "..." for "--flag"` | bad value for a real flag | correct the value |
| cert/key `no such file` | wrong `--...-cert`/`--kubeconfig` path | restore the correct path |
| `connection refused` to apiserver | apiserver itself down first | fix apiserver, then re-check |
| container never starts, nothing in logs | broken YAML in the manifest | `journalctl -u kubelet`; fix indentation |

### Fix on the node
```bash
docker exec -it $CP bash                       # exam: ssh <node>
cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
grep -n bogus kube-controller-manager.yaml     # locate the exact line
sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' kube-controller-manager.yaml
exit
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-controller-manager-$CP -w   # wait for 1/1
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Read the logs before touching anything** — guessing wastes exam minutes. The fault is almost always named verbatim.
- Use `--previous` to see the logs of the instance that *just crashed* if the current one dies too fast to log.
- **Static pod = edit the file**, never `kubectl edit`/`apply` (mirror pods are read-only).
- **No vi/nano on kind** — `sed -i` and `grep -n`. Preserve YAML indentation exactly.
- Verify with `READY 1/1`, not merely "logs look quiet." A fresh restart count resets nothing; confirm the pod is actually Running and Ready.
- If apiserver is the casualty, `kubectl` fails entirely — fall back to `crictl`/`journalctl` on the node.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get pods                                   # find the sick pod
kubectl -n kube-system logs <pod> --previous | tail                # what killed it
grep -n bogus /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-controller-manager-$CP -w       # 1/1 Ready
```
